---
title: "Dimensionality reduction"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(featR)
```

`fs_pca()` and `fs_svd()` reduce dimension without selecting features. They
replace the original columns with a few new ones, each a weighted sum of all
the inputs. You still have to measure every variable, and the new columns are
chosen without reference to any outcome: they point in the directions of
largest variance, which need not be the directions that predict anything. If
you need to name the features you keep, use one of the
[filters](filters.html), [regularization methods](regularization.html), or
[wrappers](wrappers.html) instead.

Use `fs_pca()` on a data frame when you want tidy, labeled output: variance
explained, loadings, scores next to your label columns, and a plot. Use
`fs_svd()` on a numeric matrix when you want the raw singular values and
vectors, for compression or as input to your own code.

Both functions return a plain list, not an `fs_result`, so `selected()` and
the other `fs_result` helpers do not apply.

## `fs_pca()`

Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the orthogonal directions along
which the data vary most. The first component is the direction of largest
variance, the second is the largest among directions perpendicular to the
first, and so on.

[`fs_pca()`](../reference/fs_pca.html) runs a PCA on the numeric columns of a
data frame. Character, factor, logical, and date columns are kept aside as
labels, as is the column named in `label_col`. By default it keeps two
components; set `num_pc` for more.

```{r}
pca <- fs_pca(iris, num_pc = 2, label_col = "Species")
names(pca)
pca$var_explained
pca$pc_loadings
head(pca$pca_df)
```

How to read the output:

* `var_explained` is the share of the total variance each retained component
  carries. On `iris` the first two components carry 73.0% and 22.9%, so
  together they keep about 96% of the variance in the four measurements. The
  vector sums to 1 only when you keep every component.
* `pc_loadings` holds the weights (`prcomp()`'s `rotation`), one row per input
  column. PC1 weights the petal measurements and sepal length about equally
  (0.52 to 0.58), while PC2 is mostly sepal width (-0.92). The sign of a
  component is arbitrary: a component and its negation describe the same
  direction, so compare loadings within a column, not their signs across runs.
* `pc_scores` holds each observation's coordinates on the components, and
  `pca_df` is the same scores with the label columns bound alongside.

By default columns are centered and scaled (`scale_data = TRUE`), so the PCA
runs on the correlation matrix. Leave scaling on unless every column is in the
same meaningful units; otherwise the column with the largest variance
dominates the first component. Scaling without centering
(`scale_data = TRUE, center_data = FALSE`) is an error.

### Missing values and constant columns

Before the decomposition, `fs_pca()` drops every row with a missing value in
the numeric columns, and it drops every column with zero variance with a
warning. Infinite values are an error. `meta` records what was used:

```{r}
pca$meta$n_rows_used
pca$meta$numeric_cols
```

`iris` has no missing values, so all 150 rows are used. On real data, check
`meta$n_rows_used` and `meta$rows_kept`: a few gappy columns can remove most
of the rows without an error. `num_pc` cannot exceed the number of usable
columns, or the number of usable rows minus one.

### Plotting

`fs_pca()` builds a ggplot of PC1 against PC2, colored by `label_col`,
whenever a `label_col` is supplied, at least two components are kept, and
ggplot2 is installed. The plot is returned in `$plot`; `plot = TRUE` also
prints it.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
pca$plot
```

When no plot can be built, the list has no `plot` element at all, so test
with `"plot" %in% names(pca)`.

### Large data

Below 10 million cells (rows times numeric columns), `fs_pca()` uses
`stats::prcomp()`. At or above that size it uses `bigstatsr::big_SVD()` on a
temporary file-backed matrix, if bigstatsr is installed, and computes only the
requested components; without bigstatsr it falls back to `prcomp()`. This
engine can return at most one fewer component than there are columns, so
`num_pc` equal to the number of columns is an error on large data. The
large-data engine recovers the total variance from column statistics, so
`var_explained` is still the share of the whole and not of the components
that were computed.

### Leakage

PCA never looks at the outcome, but it does learn from the rows it sees: the
centering, scaling, and loadings all come from the data. If you fit it on all
rows and then cross-validate a model on the scores, the test rows have shaped
the features. `fs_pca()` does not return the centering and scaling values or a
way to project new rows. To apply a PCA learned on training rows to test rows,
fit `stats::prcomp()` on the training rows and call `predict()` on it. See
[Validation and leakage](validation-and-leakage.html) for the general rule.

## `fs_svd()`

The singular value decomposition (SVD) factors a matrix `X` into `U D V'`:
`D` holds the singular values in decreasing order, and the columns of `U`
and `V` are the left and right singular vectors. Keeping the first `k`
triplets gives the best rank-`k` approximation of `X`.

[`fs_svd()`](../reference/fs_svd.html) is the lower-level tool. It takes a
numeric matrix `x` (or an all-numeric data frame) and returns the singular
values and vectors:

```{r}
m <- as.matrix(mtcars)
s <- fs_svd(m, n_singular_values = 3, scale_input = TRUE)
round(s$singular_values, 3)
dim(s$left_singular_vectors)
dim(s$right_singular_vectors)
```

The left singular vectors have one row per observation (32 cars) and the right
singular vectors one row per column (11 variables), each with one column per
kept triplet. By default, `n_singular_values = NULL` keeps all of them,
`min(dim(x))`.

`x` must not contain `NA`, `NaN`, or `Inf`. Unlike `fs_pca()`, `fs_svd()`
drops nothing for you, so remove or impute missing values first.

`scale_input = TRUE` (the default) centers and scales the columns first, so
the triplets factor `scale(x)`, not `x`. The column means and standard
deviations are not returned; keep them yourself if you need to map results
back to the original units. The other options are `FALSE` (use `x` as is),
`"center"`, and `"scale"`, which follows `base::scale()` and, without
centering, divides by the root mean square rather than the standard deviation.
The dividing forms stop with an error if a column has zero variance.

On centered and scaled data, the squared singular values divided by `n - 1`
are the PCA eigenvalues, so `fs_svd()` and `prcomp()` agree:

```{r}
all_sv <- fs_svd(m)$singular_values
round(all_sv^2 / (nrow(m) - 1), 4)[1:3]
round(prcomp(m, scale. = TRUE)$sdev^2, 4)[1:3]
```

### Exact or approximate

`svd_method = "auto"` uses `base::svd()` unless both of these hold: you ask
for fewer singular values than `min(dim(x))`, and the smaller dimension of the
matrix is larger than `svd_threshold` (default 100). Then it uses
`RSpectra::svds()`, which computes only the leading triplets and needs the
RSpectra package. `svd_method = "approx"` forces the approximate solver; if
you ask for all `min(dim(x))` values it falls back to the exact solver with a
message, because `RSpectra::svds()` cannot return the full set. If RSpectra
converges on fewer values than requested, featR warns and recomputes them
exactly.

On a 400 by 150 matrix, the five leading singular values from both solvers
agree to within `1e-6`:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("RSpectra", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(1)
big <- matrix(rnorm(400 * 150), 400, 150)
approx <- fs_svd(big, n_singular_values = 5, svd_method = "approx")
exact  <- fs_svd(big, n_singular_values = 5, svd_method = "exact")
all.equal(approx$singular_values, exact$singular_values, tolerance = 1e-6)
```

Singular vectors are unique only up to sign, so the two solvers, or two
platforms, can return columns with opposite signs. Compare vectors with
`abs()` or through the reconstructed matrix, not element by element.
